Substrate Master List (Pasted markdown(8).md). Product names, Master assignments, use cases, status, technology and evidence-position text are source-derived.
329 canonical entities deduplicated from 452 product-to-Master occurrences.
Rx/active treatments, devices and generic product families are retained but explicitly typed.
One canonical product/entity record; many Product_Master_Links. Repeated appearances across Masters do not create duplicate product rows.
Earliest explicit Master occurrence. all_masters contains all source-derived Master memberships.
Aggregated from source fields such as Best For, Best Use, Role and Lane.
Aggregated from source fields such as Key Technology, Strength, Strategy, Mechanism and Protection.
Preserved from source; nuanced labels have not been silently flattened.
Product URL, Image URL and current INCI require current manufacturer verification and are not guessed.
Ingredient lists must be current-formula verified before formulation-specific recommendation logic.
Product Family / Generic Type records must be resolved to specific current products before direct shopping/product matching.
Rx / Active Treatment records are clinical/intervention entities, not retail product SKUs.
Extraction is app-designer ready structurally, but not frozen as a product-science database. Review_Queue and Manufacturer_Verification are the remaining content workflow.
v0.1 — source extraction + deduplication + relationship normalization
IMPORTANT: 'NEEDS_MANUFACTURER_VERIFICATION' is deliberate. It prevents stale or guessed URLs/ingredient lists from becoming production truth.

REFORMULATION ALERT — MAJOR, AND VERY RECENT. 2026-09-05. The new C E Ferulic launched 17 August 2026, three weeks ago, and the brand has confirmed it is PHASING OUT THE OLD VERSION ENTIRELY rather than running both as separate SKUs. Substrate's most-referenced antioxidant product therefore has an unverifiable current formula: no source located this pass publishes the complete new INCI, only the three additions the brand has chosen to disclose (Carnosine 0.3%, Endophytol 1.0%, Eperuline 0.01%) under 'double patent-pending' AOX + Visible Longevity technology. CONTEXT WORTH RECORDING: the original patent expired in 2025, which is what opened the category to close structural copies (Timeless SKP-0085, Paula's Choice SKP-0084, Trader Joe's). L'Oreal had previously sued Drunk Elephant over this formula in 2020 (see SKP-0086). The brand denies the timing is patent-related. Whatever the motive, the practical consequence for Substrate is that this master's anchor product, its cheapest structural analogue, and the litigation history are all one story. TWO LEGACY REGIONAL VARIANTS also exist and are not interchangeable: the US list uses Ethoxydiglycol with Triethanolamine and Panthenol; the EU/UK list uses Dipropylene Glycol and omits both. ACTION: this record must NOT be treated as production-authoritative. Requires a follow-up pull of the printed label from a current-stock bottle. Until then, any recommendation logic keying on C E Ferulic's composition is keying on a formula that is being withdrawn.

VERIFIED 2026-09-05 — 19-ingredient list confirmed identically on Bluemercury and Dermstore. ALCOHOL SECOND AND WITCH HAZEL THIRD, IN A PIGMENTATION PRODUCT. Hyperpigmentation-prone skin is by definition prone to inflammatory pigment responses — post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is the mechanism the product exists to prevent. Denatured alcohol strips barrier lipids and witch hazel carries tannins; both are irritants, and irritation in this population produces the very outcome being treated. This is the ninth positioning-versus-composition finding and the one where the tension is most nearly self-defeating. It also contains ROSA DAMASCENA FLOWER OIL — a fragrance material — in the same product. FIVE PIGMENT PATHWAYS, GENUINELY DOSED: tranexamic acid (9th), hexylresorcinol (11th), 4-butylresorcinol (15th), glabridin (16th) and licorice root extract (17th). Unlike Topicals Faded (REV-0248) where seven actives sat at token depth, these occupy the working middle of a 19-ingredient list. FREE AHA AT POSITION SIX: lactic acid, with gluconolactone (a PHA) seventh. The seven-day photosensitivity tail fires — correctly, and importantly, because sun exposure during pigment treatment is the single worst thing a melasma patient can do. RELEVANT TO SUBSTRATE SPECIFICALLY: the brand explicitly names pigmentation from HORMONAL CHANGES. That is melasma in a perimenopausal population, stated in the marketing. Worth pairing with the low-constraint options identified at REV-0254 — this product is effective but carries alcohol, witch hazel and fragrance, so it sits at the opposite end of the tolerability range from Alastin A-Luminate and Cyspera.

ENTITY TYPE CORRECTED — REQUIRES THREE CHILD RECORDS. Confirmed across Practical Dermatology, Modern Aesthetics (interview with a board-certified dermatologist), Scientis/SENTÉ launch material and three clinic listings. WHY THE TYPE MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL HERE: this is not a routine that happens to have three steps, it is a chemically sequential protocol. Cysteamine and AHA are held apart in dual-chamber packaging and react on the skin; Neutralize exists specifically to STOP that reaction and to manage the cysteamine odour, which was the historical barrier to the ingredient. Steps cannot be substituted, reordered or omitted, and a member using only step one is not using the product as studied. A single product row cannot encode that. Recommend three child records under a system parent, with an explicit sequence constraint. UNUSUAL APPLICATION RULE: brand directs application to an UNWASHED face, and states efficacy depends on consistency of exposure over time rather than daily duration. Both run contrary to normal skincare sequencing assumptions and would be lost by a generic 'apply after cleansing' default. CLINICAL POSITIONING: marketed as achieving hydroquinone-level results without corticosteroids, retinoic acid or hydroquinone. That makes it — with Alastin A-Luminate (SKP-0119) — one of only two high-efficacy options in this master carrying none of the constraints that gate Tri-Luma, hydroquinone and the Rx retinoids. For a perimenopausal melasma population that is a meaningful position.

VERIFIED 2026-09-05 — seven-ingredient list confirmed identically across Cult Beauty UK and international, LookFantastic Germany and Sweden, and two BIOEFFECT set listings. Distinct from the EGF Power Serum (SKP-0141, twelve ingredients) — a genuine ladder pair, not a rename. IT PASSES THE POST-PROCEDURE TEST, AND THAT MATTERS FOR THE WEDGE. The rule at REV-0339 requires no preservative system AND (anhydrous OR isotonic at physiological pH). This formula has NO preservative at all — brand-stated and consistent with the seven-ingredient list — and carries sodium chloride with tromethamine as a buffer, i.e. the same saline-and-buffer construction as Tower 28 SOS (SKP-0210). Third product in the database to qualify, and by the second route. AND, CRUCIALLY, IT IS NOT CAUGHT BY THE GROWTH-FACTOR RULING. REGULATORY FLAG — EXOSOMES. VERIFIED 2026-09-05 against FDA-derived secondary sources (Dermatology Times review of FDA enforcement, two regulatory-law analyses, a PMFA Journal cosmetic-market guide). Position as of this date: (1) NO exosome product has ever completed FDA approval. Human-derived exosome products intended for therapeutic use are regulated as unapproved biological products under Section 351 of the PHS Act; because exosomes are isolated from cultured or expanded cells, FDA treats the process as more than minimal manipulation, which removes the HCT/P exemption and requires an IND or BLA. (2) TOPICAL COSMETIC USE IS PERMITTED. FDA does not pre-approve cosmetics, so an exosome-containing topical sold with appearance claims is not per se unlawful — it falls under MoCRA's safety-substantiation, facility and cosmetic-GMP requirements. (3) THE LINE IS THE CLAIM, NOT THE INGREDIENT. The moment a structure/function or therapeutic claim is made, the product becomes an unapproved new drug. FDA has issued a 2019 public safety notification, a 2020 consumer alert and repeated warning letters, with reported adverse events including serious infection, allergic reaction and tumour formation, and a documented sepsis cluster in Nebraska. (4) CRITICAL FOR SUBSTRATE'S PROCEDURE WEDGE — POST-MICRONEEDLING APPLICATION IS NOT COSMETIC USE. Regulatory analyses are explicit that because microneedling deliberately breaches the skin barrier, applying an exosome product afterwards is treated as ADMINISTRATION of an unapproved biologic rather than topical cosmetic application — regardless of a 'topical cosmetic use only' label on the bottle. Substrate's chosen entry wedge is procedure preparation and recovery. A recommendation pairing any exosome product with microneedling, or with any barrier-breaching procedure, would sit exactly on this line. ACTION: this is a Dr. Bentley ruling of the same weight as the Rx question at REV-0207, and it is more urgent because it touches the wedge rather than an adjacent category. Do not surface exosome products in any procedure-adjacent context until it is settled.

ACID VERSUS SALT FORM — A THIRD POTENCY DETERMINANT, AND IT UNIFIES THREE EARLIER FINDINGS. Ammonium lactate is the neutralised salt of lactic acid, not the free acid. At the same stated percentage a salt delivers less free acid than the parent acid, which is precisely why a 12% ammonium lactate body lotion is tolerable daily on large surface areas while a 10% free lactic acid is a once-daily facial peel. This is the same mechanism found twice already: AlphaRet and Intensive AlphaRet (SKP-0109 / SKP-0110) are identical except that glycolic acid and sodium glycolate swap positions two and three, and CeraVe's SA products declare their active as triethanolamine salicylate rather than salicylic acid. In all three cases the free-acid-versus-salt distinction is visible in the INCI and is doing the work. Combined with pH (REV-0294) and molecular size (REV-0297), that gives four inputs to exfoliation strength: concentration, acid identity, pH, and salt versus free-acid form. Percentage alone captures one of the four. SKU AMBIGUITY: the source name 'AmLactin Daily' does not identify which product. AmLactin runs at least four: Daily Moisturizing Lotion 12%, Daily Nourish 5%, Daily Nourish 12% and Intensive Healing 15%. The 12% and 5% versions differ threefold in strength and the Intensive adds ceramides and niacinamide. Scoped here to the 12% Daily Moisturizing Lotion as the flagship; confirm before production use. Sixth unversioned-name case in this database. REGULATORY DATUM WORTH RECORDING: the CIR expert panel guideline for ammonium lactate in cosmetics is ≤10% at pH ≥3.5 with sun protection. This product is 12% — above the cosmetic guidance, which is consistent with its positioning as a dermatologist-recommended treatment rather than a general moisturiser, and with prescription versions existing at 30% in some markets. Not a safety problem, but it means the product sits at the top of the OTC range and should not be treated as a bland body lotion by the engine simply because of its format. AHA RULE APPLIES (REV-0288): ammonium lactate is an AHA. Sun protection is explicitly part of the CIR condition, and the one-week post-cessation tail attaches. Notable because this is a BODY product applied to large surface areas daily — the photosensitivity consideration is larger here than for a facial serum, not smaller. Contains mineral oil third — relevant to members avoiding it, and unusual among the products verified so far.

HYDROCOLLOID DRESSING — NOT A FORMULATED PRODUCT. This is an adhesive occlusive patch, not an emulsion or solution, and it has no INCI in the ordinary sense: the material is a hydrocolloid matrix (typically CMC or pectin in a polyurethane or polyisobutylene backing). Attempting INCI verification will return nothing because there is nothing to return. MECHANISM IS PHYSICAL, NOT CHEMICAL: it absorbs exudate and maintains a moist wound environment, which is why it works on open or picked lesions and does nothing on closed comedones. It carries no active, so the OTC acne monograph 'one medication at a time' constraint (REV-0325) does NOT apply — a hydrocolloid patch can be used alongside a topical acne medication, unlike every other product in this master. That is a genuinely useful exception and would be lost if patches were modelled as ordinary products. Record as a dressing with an occlusive/absorbent mechanism. Verify the backing material and any added actives (some variants add salicylic acid or microdarts, which WOULD reintroduce the monograph constraint) rather than an ingredient list.

THREE ACIDS IN A BARRIER-REPAIR MOISTURISER — the sharpest hidden-acid case in this work. The product is explicitly positioned to hydrate a COMPROMISED BARRIER, and it contains SALICYLIC ACID (28th), PHYTIC ACID (39th) and LACTIC ACID (43rd, final). None appears in the brand's key-ingredient list. Free of fragrance, harsh alcohols, oils, parabens, silicones and sulfates. THE THREE ENZYMES RESOLVE, AND THEY ARE NOT PROPRIETARY: Plankton Extract (photolyase, repairs cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers), Arabidopsis Thaliana Extract (photolyase) and Micrococcus Lysate (UV endonuclease). The same three appear in skinbetter Alto (SKP-0094), and Plankton Extract alone drives both ISDIN Eryfotona products (SKP-0066, SKP-0068). THAT MATTERS FOR THE EQUIVALENCE WORK: DNA-repair enzymes are LICENSED raw materials, not single-company actives like Melasyl or Thiamidol (REV-0253). So analogues can exist here, and skinsort's own comparison engine already names Aspect Skincare Super PD Complex at an 80% ingredient match. The boundary drawn at REV-0256 — analogues are possible where the active is commodity, impossible where it is proprietary — holds in a fourth category. MASTER 15 IS THEREFORE A TECHNOLOGY MASTER, NOT A BRAND ONE: four products across three brands share the same enzyme set. The differentiator between them is the surrounding formulation, not the active. Worth recording, because the Master 15 evidence table recovered from the extraction artifacts asks exactly this question — enzyme identified, mechanism, evidence grade — and the answer is that the enzymes are common and the evidence attaches to the INGREDIENT rather than to any product. Grade the enzyme class once, in the Hypothesis Library, and let all four products inherit it. Contains ergothioneine and BHT as antioxidants; no fragrance and no botanical sensitiser of note beyond sandalwood extract.

REFORMULATION THAT REMOVES FOUR FRAGRANCE MOLECULES AND A DYE — the most consequential reformulation found in this work for a reactive population. The PRIOR formula ends with Ethylene Brassylate, Methyldihydrojasmonate, Isobutyl Methyl Tetrahydropyranol and Methyl Decenol — four synthetic fragrance materials — plus Caramel and YELLOW 5 (CI 19140), a synthetic dye. The CURRENT formula is marketed as fragrance-free and adds MicroDiPeptide229 and BAKUCHIOL. MECHANISM CHANGES TOO: bakuchiol is a retinol-alternative active absent from the prior formula, so the two versions are not merely a fragrance difference — the current one belongs in the retinoid-adjacent discussion and the prior one does not. Both formulas are built on Acetyl Glucosamine second — NeoGlucosamine, an amino sugar with mild keratolytic action, not an AHA. It correctly does not trigger the AHA photosensitivity rule.

Within-ladder gentleness and cross-ladder tolerability are different axes. An engine that models 'start gentle' as 'lowest rung' will send a fragrance-sensitive member to the wrong product with complete confidence. Recommend the ladder logic select the LADDER on tolerability first, then the RUNG on strength — in that order.

VERIFIED 2026-09-05 — nine-ingredient list from Beauty Bay, the brand's stated exclusive retailer for this SKU. RESOLVES THE BLOCKING AMBIGUITY ON SKP-0174: The Ordinary sells two 2% salicylic products. This anhydrous version is squalane-based with nine ingredients; the water-based Solution is a different formula entirely. They were being represented by one row, which is why SKP-0174 could not be verified. COUNTERINTUITIVE POSITIONING, AND IT IS PROBABLY RIGHT: the brand positions the ANHYDROUS version as suited to new BHA users. An oil-phase vehicle slows delivery of salicylic acid relative to an aqueous one at the same 2%, so the gentler option here is the anhydrous one. POST-PROCEDURE TEST — A THIRD OUTCOME: anhydrous, so it satisfies one branch of the rule at REV-0339, but it carries phenoxyethanol and chlorphenesin and so fails the no-preservative condition. Advanced Eye (anhydrous but preserved, fails), the rule now has four worked cases covering every combination. It is ready to build. AlphaRet vs Intensive AlphaRet — order is the only difference

The two SKUs share ~48 identical ingredients in identical sequence. The ONLY INCI-visible difference is that Glycolic Acid and Sodium Glycolate swap positions 2 and 3, implying more free acid and lower pH in Intensive.

Decisive for REV-0167 / REV-0195: ingredient ORDER is the only signal distinguishing two products sold at different strengths. Any pipeline that normalises, sorts or alphabetises ingredient lists must preserve original order as a separate field, or these two collapse into one.
Crystal Retinal — co-formulated vs layered actives

Crystal Retinal contains two vitamin C forms (THD ascorbate, 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid) while the brand simultaneously instructs users not to combine the product with vitamin C. A composition-reading conflict rule would flag the product against itself.

Conflict logic must distinguish co-formulated actives from layered ones. This is the inverse of REV-0176, where composition had to override category — together they define the boundary the rule needs to sit on.
AlphaRet is a conjugate, not a blend

Ethyl Lactyl Retinoate is a retinoid covalently bonded to lactic acid, not a retinoid mixed with an AHA. Treating it as a layered retinoid+AHA combination would wrongly predict high irritation, and AHA washout rules keyed to free acid may not apply the same way.
Add as a distinct entry in the actives library rather than decomposing it. Check whether other conjugated actives exist in the database.

Melasyl and Thiamidol are single-company actives
Melasyl (2-mercaptonicotinoyl glycine, L'Oréal) and Thiamidol (isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol, Beiersdorf) are proprietary with no generic equivalent, unlike tranexamic, kojic or azelaic acid.

Useful boundary on the equivalence-class capability (REV-0175): no low-cost structural analogue can exist where the active is proprietary. So far that capability has only been tested in categories where the active is commodity. Record proprietary-active status as a product attribute so the engine knows when not to look.

Score on evidence weight and plausible dose, never on how many mechanisms appear in a list. This is the clearest case in the database for that rule.
Cyspera is a sequential system, not a product

Three chemically dependent steps: cysteamine and AHA held apart in dual-chamber packaging and reacting on skin, then Neutralize specifically to stop that reaction and manage odour, then Boost. Steps cannot be reordered, substituted or omitted. Brand also directs application to UNWASHED skin.

Retyped to Multi-step System / Kit. Needs three child records under a system parent with an explicit sequence constraint. The unwashed-skin instruction would be silently overwritten by any generic "apply after cleansing" default.

Confirms the equivalence-class boundary is drawn on ACTIVE TYPE, not on product category. That is the more useful formulation: the engine can decide whether to search for an analogue by checking one attribute on the active, rather than by category heuristics.

EXOSOMES — ruling needed, and it touches the wedge

No exosome product has FDA approval; human-derived exosomes for therapeutic use are unapproved biologics requiring an IND. Topical cosmetic use IS permitted under MoCRA — the line is the claim, not the ingredient. But regulatory analyses are explicit that applying an exosome product after microneedling counts as ADMINISTRATION of an unapproved biologic, not cosmetic use, because the procedure breaches the barrier — regardless of a "topical cosmetic use only" label.

Substrate's entry wedge is procedure prep and recovery, so this sits directly on the wedge rather than beside it. More urgent than REV-0207. Do not surface exosome products in any procedure-adjacent context until Dr. Bentley rules. Affects SKP-0151, 0152, 0153 and any future exosome SKU.
Growth-factor and conditioned-media products — same ruling scope

SkinMedica TNS, Neocutis, AnteAGE and CALECIM derive actives from cultured human cells or conditioned media. Longer market history and no comparable enforcement, but the same claim-versus-ingredient line and the same post-procedure question, since these are routinely marketed for use after microneedling and laser.

Include in the same Bentley ruling rather than treating as ordinary cosmetics. Separately capture human/animal-derived sourcing as a member-preference attribute, distinct from the regulatory question.
Alastin Restorative Skin Complex had THREE records

Procedures and devices belong in the Procedure Engine
PDL, KTP laser, IPL and professional mandelic peels were typed as Finished Products in the product database.

Procedures are the INPUT side of washout and recovery logic — the thing a member has had done that constrains what they can then apply. Modelling them as products inverts that relationship. Move to the Procedure Engine and reference them from there.
Two ORAL systemic drugs sit in a topical product database
Low-dose doxycycline (SKP-0250) and low-dose minocycline (SKP-0251) are oral systemic antibiotics used for rosacea, not topicals. They were typed Finished Product.

Retyped Rx, but the deeper question is whether systemic agents belong in a topical product database at all. If Substrate is to represent them — reasonable, since they affect skin outcomes and interact with photosensitising topicals — they need a distinct entity type and their own constraint model. Doxycycline in particular is photosensitising, which interacts directly with the retinoid and AHA sun-sensitivity rules already logged.
The lone Device row was a table fragment, not a device

"Placebo controlled", with notes "Yes/No; Objective 3D imaging" — the tenth fragment of the Master 18 evidence table. It was typed Device by the source extraction, and the entity-type audit missed it because that audit EXCLUDED rows already typed Device, Rx or Family.

Every exclusion in a data-quality check is an assumption about data already proven unreliable — run future audits with no exclusions and filter afterwards.

Four SYSTEMIC agents sit in a topical product database
Spironolactone (oral anti-androgen) and combined oral contraceptives (exogenous hormone therapy) in Master 10, plus low-dose oral doxycycline and minocycline in Master 13. None is a topical.

Spironolactone and COCs act on the exact axis Substrate's thesis rests on. A member taking either has a pharmacologically altered hormonal profile, which changes how her biomarkers should be READ, not just which products suit her. That makes them relevant as CONTEXT the platform must know about while never recommending. The database cannot currently distinguish "input to interpretation" from "candidate recommendation" — it needs to.

Rows correctly typed Product Family or Rx but still carrying the default "EXTRACTED — NEEDS DATABASE QA" status have been given proper NOT APPLICABLE statuses, so they no longer appear to be awaiting verification.

Growth factors split three ways, not one

BIOEFFECT's EGF and KGF are recombinant proteins expressed in barley, declared as sh-Oligopeptide-1 and sh-Polypeptide-3. That is materially different from SkinMedica TNS, Neocutis, AnteAGE and CALECIM, whose actives are harvested from cultured human cells or conditioned media.

BIOEFFECT must NOT inherit the growth-factor regulatory flag at REV-0260 — plant-expressed recombinant peptides carry neither the Section 351 questions nor the human-sourcing concern. The actives library should distinguish synthetic peptides, plant-expressed recombinants, and human-cell-derived material. Only the third carries regulatory and sourcing weight, and a single "growth factor" category would collapse all three.
Cult Beauty copy names two ingredients that are not in the product
The description states the serum contains hyaluronic acid, niacinamide and ferulic acid. Neither niacinamide nor ferulic acid appears in the 12-ingredient INCI printed on the same page.

Third source-reliability finding, and the first where the error and the correct data sit on the SAME page. A pipeline reading description prose rather than the INCI block would ingest two ingredients that do not exist. Rule: parse INCI blocks only, never marketing prose — including from otherwise reliable retailers.
BIOEFFECT EGF Serum is a separate product
The original EGF Serum and the EGF Power Serum are distinct formulations; brand copy describes the Power Serum as the original "but better".

Do not inherit SKP-0141's ingredient list. Verify separately. Fourth instance in this database of a brand running a base/intensified pair that must not be conflated, after AlphaRet, Crystal Retinal and the SkinCeuticals retinols.
The post-injectable product was missing from the database

ALASTIN INhance Post-Injection Serum — built specifically for dermal filler recovery — had no record, while ALASTIN Restorative Skin Complex had three. Substrate's thesis runs to filler longevity and its wedge is procedure prep and recovery.

Stub created at SKP-0337. Check whether the rest of the TriHex line (TransFORM Body, ReFORM & RePAIR) is also absent. The gap is worth noting as a pattern: the database over-represents daily-use products and under-represents procedure-linked ones, which is the inverse of the wedge.
Procedure-linked recommendations need a date, not a skin state

A practitioner protocol recorded with this product pairs three ALASTIN SKUs across three phases: Regenerating Skin Nectar starting two weeks BEFORE a filler appointment, INhance after it, Restorative Skin Complex once healed.

Pre-loading cannot be expressed by a product row or by current skin state — the recommendation has to fire on a SCHEDULED FUTURE procedure date. The Orchestration Engine needs procedure dates as an input, and products need a procedure-phase attribute (pre / immediate-post / recovery / maintenance).
Anhydrous construction is what makes a product post-procedure-eligible

Regenerating Skin Nectar is water-free and preservative-free by design: no water removes both the need for preservatives and the sting that water-based products cause on raw skin, which is why it can be applied immediately after a barrier-breaching procedure.

Record anhydrous / preservative-free / compromised-barrier-suitable as a formulation ATTRIBUTE, not a product note. It is the property that determines post-procedure eligibility at all, and it is derivable from the INCI for every product in the database.
The manufacturer itself defers procedure timing to the clinician
ALASTIN's own directions state that procedure care usage varies by procedure and should follow the treating health care provider's direction, rather than specifying a schedule.

A useful precedent for where Substrate draws its own line, and brand-stated rather than inferred. Worth citing in the Bentley discussion: the manufacturer of the flagship pre/post-procedure product declines to give procedure-linked timing without a clinician.
Marketing copy contradicts the INCI — fourth instance
An authorised reseller lists niacinamide and hyaluronic acid among this product's active ingredients. Neither appears in the 22-ingredient INCI.

Fourth instance, now spanning dermfnd, well.co.uk, Cult Beauty and an authorised physician reseller. Authorised-reseller status does not protect against it. Reinforces REV-0273: parse INCI blocks only.
Copper peptides and vitamin C — a chemical conflict, not a tolerance one
Copper ions inactivate ascorbic acid. NIOD CAIS3 carries 1% copper tripeptide-1; Master 05 holds eight L-ascorbic acid products.

This conflict holds regardless of member sensitivity because it is chemical rather than tolerance-based — the two simply cancel. Distinguish CHEMICAL incompatibility from TOLERANCE conflict in the engine; they need different messaging and different override rules. Note also the layered-versus-co-formulated boundary at REV-0221 applies.
Active count and active POSITION are two different signals

CAIS3 carries six peptides at positions 3–8, consistent with real dosing. Topicals Faded (REV-0248) carries seven actives spread from position 4 to 20, consistent with token inclusion. Counting actives alone would rank them similarly.
The engine needs both signals together: how many actives, and how high they sit. Either alone produces the wrong ranking. This pair is a good regression test for whatever scoring approach gets built.

NIOD CAIS3 (activator poured in and shaken before first use), Drunk Elephant C-Firma Fresh (powder into base, 6-month post-activation window) and Cyspera (dual-chamber, cysteamine and AHA reacting on skin). All three have a composition that differs before and after activation.

Add a formulation attribute for user-activated products, with an activation-date field where a post-activation window exists. Currently handled as three separate product notes, which means the pattern is invisible to the engine.
Source name carried no generation. NIOD has run at least three CAIS versions; the original is 1% copper tripeptide-1 alone, CAIS 3 1:1 adds 1% pure GHK plus three further peptides.
Scoped to CAIS 3 as current. Fifth instance of a brand version pair that must not be conflated, after AlphaRet, Crystal Retinal, the SkinCeuticals retinols and BIOEFFECT.
Renames and version pairs need opposite handling

"Buffet + Copper Peptides 1%" was renamed to "Multi-Peptide + Copper Peptides 1%" — one product, two names, still listed both ways by retailers. That is the inverse of the version pairs at REV-0283, where two genuinely different products share a name stem.

A name-similarity duplicate check would MERGE a version pair (wrong) and SPLIT a rename (also wrong). Both failure modes are live in this database. Duplicate resolution needs the INCI as the tiebreaker, not the name: identical lists mean rename, materially different lists mean version pair.
Visible product identity as an adherence signal
The formula is visibly blue because of the copper peptides — brand-stated, and one of very few products in this database with an observable identity marker.

A member can confirm they have the right product, and notice degradation, without reading a label. The Outcome Engine could use appearance as a low-effort adherence and product-integrity check. Worth capturing appearance as a field where it is distinctive — also relevant to C E Ferulic, where brand copy already explains expected darkening.
Single-use formats break the usage schema
SkinCeuticals Biocellulose Masque is a single-use sheet product. The usage fields added at v3.6 — frequency, post_open_shelf_life, time_of_day — assume a repeat-use container.

Decide how single-use formats are handled before verifying. Dose is fixed by the sheet rather than the member, frequency is occasional rather than daily, and there is no post-opening window because the product is consumed in one use.

All 22 original rows plus SKP-0333 and SKP-0337 now carry an explicit status. Verified or partial: SKP-0138 (flagged), 0140 (queued), 0141, 0146, 0154, 0156. Regulatory-blocked: 0139, 0142, 0143, 0144, 0150, 0151, 0152, 0153. Merged: 0148, 0149, 0157. Repaired: 0145. Ambiguous: 0147. Created: 0333, 0337.

Outstanding: INCI tails for SKP-0154 and SKP-0141's sibling SKP-0140; SKP-0158 pending the single-use decision; SKP-0333 Medik8 Liquid Peptides and SKP-0337 INhance both need verification. The eight regulatory-blocked rows wait on the exosome and growth-factor rulings at REV-0259 and REV-0260.
The AHA one-week photosensitivity tail is DERIVABLE, not per-product

The sunburn alert found on skinbetter AlphaRet Clearing Serum (REV-0239) — sun sensitivity persisting for a week after stopping — is the US-mandated standard AHA warning, not brand-specific copy. It applies to every product containing a free AHA.

Derive the seven-day post-cessation photosensitivity tail from composition rather than reading it off each label. Directly relevant to the Procedure Engine: a member who stops an exfoliant before a procedure remains photosensitive for a week. Master 09 holds at least twelve AHA products this applies to.
A member-adjustable dose breaks fixed-concentration assumptions
The Ordinary directs that Lactic Acid 10% "can be diluted with other treatments to reduce strength until skin develops tolerance" — a brand-sanctioned variable dose.

Effective concentration is not a fixed product attribute here. Any cumulative-acid or exposure calculation assuming 10% will overstate it for a member following the brand's own titration advice. Add a dilutable flag; this is the first product found where the member sets the dose.
The Ordinary renames often enough to break name matching

Second suspected rename from this brand in two masters: Buffet became Multi-Peptide + Copper Peptides (SKP-0154), and Glycolic Acid 7% Toning Solution appears alongside Glycolic Acid 7% Exfoliating Toner at the same ingredient count.

Test case for the REV-0284 tiebreaker — but note a matching ingredient COUNT is not a matching LIST, so pull both before deciding. Consider flagging the whole brand for INCI-first rather than name-first resolution.
AHA and BHA are different classes — REV-0288 must not over-apply

The mandated sunburn alert with its one-week post-cessation tail attaches to ALPHA hydroxy acids only. Salicylic acid is a beta hydroxy acid and carries no such requirement; PC 2% BHA asks for daytime sunscreen but states no post-use window.

Write the derivation at REV-0288 on FREE AHA, never on "exfoliant". Applied to BHA it would produce seven-day washout windows that are wrong. Also note AlphaRet Clearing Serum's one-week tail comes from its lactic acid, not its salicylic acid — a product carrying both needs the AHA rule for the right reason.
The highest-acid at-home peel was missing

The Ordinary AHA 30% + BHA 2% Peeling Solution had no record. At 30% combined AHA plus 2% BHA, rinsed after ten minutes, it sits closer to a superficial chemical peel than a leave-on exfoliant, and it is cheap and unsupervised.

Stub created at SKP-0338. The database holds professional peels as a Procedure row and low-strength leave-on acids as products, with nothing between — this occupies that gap. A member may have used it days before a procedure without calling it a peel. Check for other high-strength at-home peels similarly absent.
Paula's Choice directs first-time BHA users to start every other day at night for a few weeks before increasing — following The Ordinary's dilution instruction at REV-0289.

Two different brand-sanctioned titration mechanisms now found: dilution (concentration) and frequency ramp (exposure). The ramp_required field created at v3.6 was left unpopulated as member-dependent, but where the BRAND states a schedule it is product-intrinsic and can be captured without waiting on the Bentley ruling.
The database has no pH field, and for acids that breaks ranking

pH determines what fraction of an acid is present in free, active form. A 10% glycolic at pH 4.5 is materially gentler than a 10% glycolic at pH 3.2. Drunk Elephant publishes its pH (and sources disagree on whether it is 3.5 or 3.8, a difference that straddles glycolic acid's pKa); most brands do not publish it at all.

Add a formulation_pH field, populated where brands publish it and left null otherwise. Any exfoliation-strength, cumulative-acid or procedure-washout logic built on percentage alone will misrank Master 09 — and the null case has to be handled explicitly rather than treated as average, because the products that do not publish pH are the majority.
Framboos pH reported as both 3.5 and 3.8
Three retailers quote the brand's own "ideal pH" sentence with two different values. Around glycolic acid's pKa of roughly 3.8, that difference changes the free-acid fraction substantially.

Confirm against brand packaging. The same product cannot be both, and this is the one product in the master where pH is published at all — getting it wrong here undermines the case for collecting it elsewhere.
SkinCeuticals routinely embeds acids in non-exfoliant products

Third instance in the line: Silymarin CF carries 0.5% salicylic acid as an antioxidant serum (REV-0176), Discoloration Defense carries HEPES, and Glycolic 10 Renew carries salicylic acid at position 20 alongside its glycolic.

Composition-based washout logic is essential rather than optional for this brand. Worth checking the rest of the SkinCeuticals range in the database for the same pattern before any category-based rule is trusted.
Exfoliation strength needs molecular size AND pH, not just percentage

Mandelic 10% at pH 4.0 is gentle for two independent reasons: the larger molecule penetrates more slowly, and the higher pH leaves less acid in free form. Ranked on stated percentage alone it would sit level with a 10% glycolic, which is wrong on both counts.

An exfoliation-strength model needs acid identity (molecular size, pKa) and pH alongside concentration. Second published pH in the master, and it makes the REV-0294 field request concrete: with mandelic at 4.0 and Framboos at 3.5–3.8, the two data points already span a meaningful range.
The Ordinary Salicylic 2% — two products AND two versions

The brand sells "Salicylic Acid 2% Solution" and "Salicylic Acid 2% ANHYDROUS Solution" side by side, plus a 2% Masque and a 0.5% Body Serum. Separately, skinsort holds the Solution at 11 ingredients and an "old" version at 14.

An anhydrous vehicle behaves differently from a water-based one — penetration, tolerability and layering all change. Identify both the SKU and the current version before verifying. Third The Ordinary naming problem in three masters; make INCI-first resolution a standing rule for this brand.
Dilution is a brand-level convention, not per-product
The same "can be diluted with other treatments to reduce strength until skin develops a tolerance" instruction appears on both Lactic Acid 10% and Mandelic Acid 10%.

The dilutable flag proposed at REV-0289 can be set at brand level for The Ordinary's acid range rather than product by product. Check whether the convention extends to the Glycolic and Salicylic products when those are verified.
Mandelic acid is derived from bitter almonds. The finished acid is not a nut protein, but The Ordinary flags nut-free status on other products, so the question is live for its customers.
Surface for nut-allergy screening rather than treating as a non-issue. Applies to every mandelic product in this master, including Face Reality Mandelic Serum and the professional mandelic peels row.
Acid vs salt form — the fourth potency input, and it unifies three findings

Ammonium lactate (AmLactin) and triethanolamine salicylate (CeraVe SA) are neutralised salts, not free acids, and deliver less free acid at the same stated percentage. This is the same mechanism that makes AlphaRet and Intensive AlphaRet differ (glycolic acid vs sodium glycolate swapping positions 2 and 3) — the only INCI-visible difference between those two SKUs.

Exfoliation strength has four inputs: concentration, acid identity (size and pKa), pH, and salt versus free-acid form. Percentage alone captures one. All four are derivable from the INCI, so this is buildable now rather than needing new data collection. It also explains why a 12% body lotion is daily-tolerable while a 10% facial acid is a once-daily peel.
AHA exposure is larger on the body, not smaller

AmLactin is a 12% AHA applied daily to large body surface areas. The one-week post-cessation photosensitivity tail applies, and total exposure is proportionally greater than for any facial serum in this master.

Body AHA products should not be treated as lower-risk than facial ones because of their format. Relevant to procedure washout: a member who stops a facial acid but continues a body AHA is still within the photosensitivity window.
AmLactin 12% sits above the CIR cosmetic guideline

The CIR expert panel guideline for ammonium lactate in cosmetics is ≤10% at pH ≥3.5 with sun protection. This product is 12%, consistent with its dermatologist-recommended positioning and with 30% prescription versions existing in some markets.

Not a safety problem, but it places the product at the top of the OTC range. The engine should not treat it as a bland body moisturiser because of its lotion format — format and potency are independent here.

Source name "AmLactin Daily" does not identify which of at least four products is meant: Daily Moisturizing 12%, Daily Nourish 5%, Daily Nourish 12%, Intensive Healing 15%. The 12% and 5% differ threefold.

Scoped to the 12% Daily Moisturizing Lotion; confirm. Sixth case after AlphaRet, Crystal Retinal, SkinCeuticals Retinol, BIOEFFECT and NIOD — unversioned names are the single most common naming defect in this database.
The AHA rule must key on AHA-as-exfoliant, not AHA presence

Citric acid is an alpha hydroxy acid and appears at the END of dozens of ingredient lists across this database as a pH adjuster — including in Daily Microfoliant, an enzymatic exfoliant with no AHA exfoliation claim. A rule written as "contains an AHA" would fire the one-week photosensitivity tail on a large share of the database, most of it wrongly.

Third and most important refinement to REV-0288. The rule needs AHA identity AND a position or concentration threshold: a stated percentage, or placement high in the list. Citric acid low in a list is a buffer, not an exfoliant. Getting this wrong would not produce a few bad answers — it would make the photosensitivity flag meaningless by firing everywhere.
An earlier Daily Microfoliant formula contains HYDROLYZED WHEAT PROTEIN; the current one does not. A member avoiding gluten topically would get opposite answers depending on which version she holds.

Clearest case yet for why reformulation flags need a resolution date rather than staying open indefinitely — this one changes an allergen answer, not a marketing claim. Confirm which version is currently shipping and record the changeover.

Free AHA (lactic, glycolic, mandelic), AHA salt (ammonium lactate), BHA (salicylic, and its triethanolamine salt), and enzymatic (papain). Each has different photosensitivity, washout and tolerance behaviour.

Add a mechanism sub-type field, the same conclusion reached for Master 05 at REV-0203. "Exfoliant" as a single category cannot carry correct rules — papain needs no sun warning, free AHA needs a week, and the salts sit between.
Tatcha sells The Rice Polish as Classic, Gentle, Deep and Calming, differing in abrasive and enzymatic load. The source name identifies none.
Resolve before verifying — Gentle and Deep are not interchangeable for a reactive member. Unversioned names now account for seven records across six masters.
The database systematically misses BOTH ENDS of intensity ladders

Missing gentlest rungs: Medik8 Crystal Retinal 1 (REV-0224), SkinCeuticals Retinol 0.3 (REV-0231), Paula's Choice Calm 1% BHA (new). Missing strongest: The Ordinary AHA 30% + BHA 2% (REV-0292), Paula's Choice 25% AHA + 2% BHA Peel (new). Five instances across three masters, and the middle rungs are consistently present.

This is exactly backwards for Substrate. The gentlest rung is what a reactive perimenopausal member should start on, and the strongest is what she may have used unsupervised before a procedure. The middle is the least decision-relevant part of each ladder. Audit every ladder in the database for both endpoints before further verification — the gap is systematic, not incidental.
Paula's Choice runs eleven exfoliant SKUs; the database holds three

The range includes 2% BHA in Liquid, Gel, Lotion and Toner forms, 8% AHA Gel, 25% AHA + 2% BHA Peel, 6% Mandelic + 2% Lactic, CLEAR Regular and Extra Strength, Calm 1% BHA, and Resist Daily Pore-Refining. The database holds the 8% AHA Gel, the 2% BHA Liquid and an unspecified CLEAR.

Decide which the platform carries. Note the vehicle variants (liquid, gel, lotion, toner) at the same 2% are a distinct problem from the strength variants — vehicle changes tolerability and layering without changing the acid.

CLEAR Anti-Redness Exfoliating Solution exists in Regular and Extra strength as separate SKUs. The source name specifies neither. This row also absorbed the duplicate merged from Master 10 at REV-0247.
Resolving the strength also settles which product that merged duplicate referred to.
My own annotations in product_name defeated my own duplicate detector

Across earlier passes I appended flags like "— NAME REQUIRES CONFIRMATION" and "— STRENGTH REQUIRES CONFIRMATION" directly to product_name on 8 rows. Name normalisation in the duplicate sweep stripped some suffixes but not these, so an annotated row could no longer match its unannotated twin.

All 8 annotations moved into notes; product_name restored to the clean product name. Rule going forward: product_name holds the product name only. Status and caveats belong in notes and review_status. This is the second time a data-quality tool has been defeated by an assumption I introduced myself, after the entity-type exclusions at REV-0269.
Naturium azelaic duplicate — found only after the annotation fix
SKP-0130 (Master 07) and SKP-0204 (Master 10) are the same Naturium Azelaic Topical Acid 10%. The pair was invisible to every prior sweep because SKP-0130 carried my annotation suffix.

Merged into SKP-0130; carry Master 10 membership via Product_Master_Links. Azelaic acid legitimately spans pigmentation, acne and rosacea (REV-0257) — that should be one record with three memberships, not three records. Re-run the duplicate sweep now that names are clean.

SKP-0278 ("Yes/No") and SKP-0280 ("AM/PM") are Master 15 evidence-table cells. The entity-type detector let them through because it required a capitalised word after the first, which both satisfy while carrying no product identity.

Retyped as extraction artifacts, bringing the total to twelve. The detector heuristic has now failed in four distinct ways across this session — treat every "clean" sweep as provisional until the underlying import is rebuilt.
SKP-0278, SKP-0280  [rows DELETED from Products_Canonical — see Evidence_Fragments]
Brand column backfilled to enable brand-level rules
The brand field was empty on 27 of 222 finished products, which blocked ladder detection and any brand-level rule. 18 have been backfilled from the product-name prefix.

Brand-level rules already needed: alphabetical ingredient ordering (skinbetter, Blue Lizard), INCI-first resolution (The Ordinary), house alcohol/glycol load (SkinCeuticals), embedded unadvertised acids (SkinCeuticals). None of those can be applied while brand is null. Remaining nulls are products whose name does not begin with the brand — resolve manually.
Delivery system is a fifth potency determinant

Naturium's 2% salicylic acid is microencapsulated for slow release; Paula's Choice 2% BHA is not. Same acid, same stated percentage, different effective potency — and nothing in the concentration says so.

Add delivery system (encapsulated / microencapsulated / free) alongside concentration, acid identity, pH and salt form. Five inputs now, all derivable from INCI plus brand copy. Encapsulation also appears in the retinoid master (CeraVe encapsulated retinol, Medik8 cyclodextrin), so this is not exfoliant-specific.
The AHA one-week derivation confirmed by retailer directions

Escentual's listing for The Ordinary Lactic Acid 5% states plainly: 'Use sunscreen for a week after using.' The seven-day tail this database derives from composition is stated outright in the category's own directions.

Good validation of REV-0288 — the derived rule matches what the category already tells people. Worth citing when the rule is reviewed, since a derived constraint that matches independent published directions is far easier to defend than one asserted from first principles.
Citric acid at position six — the closest call for the buffer rule

Naturium BHA carries citric acid sixth, high enough to be functional, alongside a 'bioactive fruit acids' claim and three Microcitrus extracts. The derivation classifies it as a buffer, correctly, because citric acid is not on the exfoliating-AHA list.

Flagged rather than overridden — loosening the rule for one product would reintroduce the false positives quantified at REV-0305 (20 buffer instances against 11 genuine tails). If citric acid ever needs to count, it should be by explicit per-product override, not by relaxing the class rule.
Physical abrasion added to the mechanism classifier

FAB KP Bump Eraser leads with PUMICE and carries free glycolic and lactic acids — a mechanical scrub and a 10% AHA treatment simultaneously. The classifier had no category for physical abrasion, so the product would have been modelled as acid-only.

Added, gated on the abrasive appearing in the first four positions so texture additives are not miscounted. Physical abrasion carries no photosensitivity of its own but compounds barrier disruption with acids, and is a hard post-procedure exclusion that no acid rule would catch.
Five fruit extracts are not five acids

Naturium Glycolic Resurfacing Gel carries bilberry, sugarcane, orange, lemon, sugar maple and Microcitrus extracts at positions 7–12 — the classic 'natural AHA' marketing complex. They contribute negligible acid; the 10% glycolic at position 2 is the exfoliating agent.
Same class of error as the citric acid buffer case (REV-0305): an ingredient-matching engine would read six acids where there is one. Botanical fruit extracts should never count toward acid load.
Ninth unversioned name, and the difference is fragrance
FAB KP Bump Eraser exists as Original and Fresh Strawberry. The strawberry version adds strawberry extract, isopropyl myristate and four fragrance molecules absent from the Original.
Scoped to Original. The variant axis here is exactly the one a reactive member cares about — an unversioned name would give a fragrance-avoidant member a four-allergen product.
Abrasive classifier tightened after a false positive

The first version of the physical-abrasion rule included nylon-12 and alumina, which fired on Colorescience Sport Stick (SKP-0074) — a sunscreen where nylon-12 is a texture agent and alumina is a titanium dioxide coating, neither an exfoliant.

Narrowed to unambiguous abrasives (pumice, walnut shell, apricot seed powder, sodium bicarbonate, diatomaceous earth) plus microcrystalline cellulose only at position 1. Caught within one run because the classifier output was inspected rather than assumed — worth keeping that check on every derivation change.
My annotations in data fields have now broken three separate derivations

Source annotations prefixed into ingredient_list — e.g. "CURRENT (Beauty Bay, three storefronts): " — contain commas, so comma-splitting shifts every ingredient position. That silently dropped Dermalogica Daily Microfoliant from the physical-abrasion class. It follows the same failure as annotations in product_name defeating the duplicate sweep (REV-0312) and entity-type exclusions hiding the Device artifact (REV-0269). 40 rows carry such prefixes.

Fixed by stripping leading annotations at derivation time rather than by editing the data, so provenance stays visible to a human reader while position analysis sees a clean list. The general rule: any field a derivation reads must be normalised at read time, because annotations WILL be added. This is the third instance — treat it as a design constraint, not a recurring accident.
(40 rows carry leading source annotations in ingredient_list; fix applied at derivation-read time, not by editing the data — SKP-0179 is the regression case)
ExfoliKate combines five exfoliation mechanisms and a phototoxic oil

Free lactic acid (2nd), silica abrasion (3rd), salicylic acid (14th), bromelain and papain (28th, 29th) and retinyl palmitate (30th) — five pathways. Plus bergamot fruit oil, which is phototoxic, and eleven fragrance materials including four declared allergens, applied to freshly abraded skin.

Bergamot phototoxicity is an ACUTE risk distinct from the AHA seven-day tail, and the two compound. Exclude for reactive, post-procedure and compromised-barrier members. This is the clearest case in the database of a widely-sold product whose positioning gives no indication it is unsuitable.
Silica added to the abrasive rule, gated to the top three positions
Silica is the abrasive in ExfoliKate at position 3, but appears as a texture agent and mattifier throughout the sunscreen and primer categories where it must not count.

Gated at position ≤3 rather than ≤4 to stay clear of the sunscreen false positives that the first abrasive rule produced (REV-0322). Classifier output inspected after the change, per the standing check.
The acne monograph forbids stacking topical acne medications

CeraVe Acne Control Gel carries the printed OTC warning: irritation and dryness are more likely if another topical acne medication is used at the same time, and if irritation occurs, use only ONE topical acne medication at a time. This is standard US acne-monograph labelling, not brand copy.

Master 10 holds 27 unverified acne rows plus benzoyl peroxide, adapalene, sulfur and salicylic products already recorded. This constraint applies across all of them and is regulatory rather than advisory. Build it before verifying Master 10, so the products are recorded against a rule that already exists — the same order that worked for the AHA tail.
Hidden AHAs inside an acne product

Glycolic acid fourth and lactic acid fifth, both free, in a product marketed and categorised as a 2% salicylic acid acne treatment. It carries a seven-day photosensitivity tail that neither its name nor its category suggests.

Fifth instance of the hidden-acid pattern. Notable because acne products are used by younger and often sun-exposed members, and because the AHA tail here is derived correctly only by reading composition.
The AHA seven-day tail now confirmed twice from printed labelling
CeraVe's printed Drug Facts panel states the one-week post-cessation sun warning in full, independently of the Escentual confirmation at REV-0317.

Two independent printed confirmations of a rule this database derives from composition. That is a strong evidentiary position for the Bentley review — the derivation reproduces mandated labelling rather than asserting something new.

Token-overlap matching across all masters surfaced 127 candidate pairs, against zero found by exact-name matching. 32 were confirmed by hand as the same product under different names and merged. The pattern: filler words differ ("PanOxyl Acne Creamy Wash" vs "PanOxyl Creamy Wash"), or the same product was entered separately in each master it belongs to (Paula's Choice 2% BHA in Exfoliation AND Acne; Beauty of Joseon Relief Sun in Sunscreen AND Acne).

Exact-name matching was never going to find these. Run fuzzy matching on every import. Note PanOxyl had THREE records for one 4% wash and THREE for one 10% wash; adapalene had FIVE across four masters.

The same sweep flags Crystal Retinal 3/6/10/20, SkinCeuticals Retinol 0.3/0.5/1.0, Face Shield Flex/Glow/Bronze, EltaMD UV Clear/Daily/Sport, the three AlphaRets, The Ordinary Lactic 5%/10%, Medik8 C-Tetra pair, BIOEFFECT EGF pair and the Paula's Choice acid range as high-similarity pairs. All are genuinely distinct products.

Fuzzy matching CANNOT be run unsupervised — it would collapse every intensity ladder in the database, which is exactly the structure Substrate needs most (REV-0309). The discriminator is whether the names differ by a strength token (sibling) or by filler words (duplicate). Recorded so a future automated pass does not undo this.
Cross-master entry is the root cause, not sloppy naming

Most merged pairs are the same product entered once per master it appears in — Paula's Choice 2% BHA in Exfoliation and Acne, Beauty of Joseon Relief Sun in Sunscreen and Acne, Tower 28 SOS in Moisturizers and Rosacea, AmLactin in Exfoliation and Body.

The source document is organised by master, so a product serving three concerns was written three times. Product_Master_Links exists precisely to express that as one record with three memberships. Every future import must resolve to canonical product first, then attach masters — not the reverse.
The AHA position threshold gave opposite answers on two CeraVe products, both correct

Glycolic acid sits 4th in CeraVe Acne Control Gel (tail fires) and 13th in CeraVe Acne Foaming Cream Cleanser (tail does not). Same brand, same acid, different function — exfoliant in one, pH adjuster in an alkaline-buffered cleanser in the other.

The cleanest validation yet of the position threshold at REV-0305. A presence-based rule would have fired on both; a brand-level rule would have fired on both. Only position separates them, and it separates them correctly.

A chemical incompatibility, not a tolerance issue — the two cancel regardless of skin robustness. Master 05 holds eight L-ascorbic acid products; Master 10 now holds several benzoyl peroxide products.

Second chemical incompatibility after copper peptides and vitamin C (REV-0280). Both share the structure: no override possible, different messaging from an irritation warning. Worth generalising as an incompatibility CLASS in the engine rather than two one-off rules.
BPO sun instruction is same-day, not a seven-day tail

PanOxyl directs applying sunscreen after use if going outside, and stopping both products if sensitivity develops. Benzoyl peroxide is not an AHA and carries no post-cessation photosensitivity window.
Record the distinction explicitly so the AHA seven-day tail and the BPO same-day instruction are not collapsed into one sun rule. Master 10 mixes both classes freely.
10% BPO is not simply stronger than 4%

Published comparative evidence generally finds little added efficacy above roughly 2.5% benzoyl peroxide while irritation rises with concentration. PanOxyl 10% has a plain base; CeraVe 4% carries three ceramides, cholesterol, phytosphingosine and niacinamide.

For a perimenopausal member with declining barrier function, the base composition likely matters more than the BPO percentage. Grade this properly in the Hypothesis Library rather than letting concentration imply ranking — it is the same trap as active-count proxying for efficacy (REV-0248).
Chemical incompatibility built as a derived field

Copper peptides x L-ascorbic acid (REV-0280) and benzoyl peroxide x L-ascorbic acid (REV-0333) were logged as two separate findings. Both are now derived from INCI into a chemical_incompatibility field, with ester forms of vitamin C explicitly excluded because they are not affected.

Chemical incompatibility has no tolerance override — unlike every other conflict in this database, a robust member cannot simply proceed. It needs different messaging and different precedence in the Orchestration Engine.
Formulation simplicity should be a first-class attribute

De La Cruz Sulfur Ointment has TWO ingredients: sulfur 10% and PEG-7 glyceryl cocoate. Sunday Riley Saturn delivers the same active at the same dose with 34. Every exclusion gate this database has built passes trivially on the first.

For a member who has failed multiple products on tolerability, a two-ingredient formulation is qualitatively different from a well-tolerated thirty-ingredient one — there is almost nothing left to react to. Add an ingredient-count or simplicity attribute; it is derivable now and directly useful for the reactive segment.
A brand claims its sulfur mask treats HORMONAL acne
Sunday Riley states Saturn addresses hormonal acne and acne rosacea. Sulfur is keratolytic and antimicrobial; it does not act on hormonal drivers.

Hormonal acne is Substrate's core territory, which makes this the exact claim language the platform must not reproduce even when quoting a brand. Route the CLAIM to Dr. Bentley as an example, separately from any decision about the product.
Post-procedure eligibility has two formulation routes, not one

Alastin Regenerating Skin Nectar qualifies by being anhydrous — no water, so no preservative and no sting on raw skin. Tower 28 SOS qualifies the opposite way — isotonic aqueous, no preservative system, skin-compatible pH 4.5, essentially wound-irrigation chemistry.

The attribute proposed at REV-0276 cannot be "anhydrous". Derive it as: no preservative system AND (anhydrous OR isotonic at physiological pH). Both branches now have a worked example in the database, which is enough to specify the rule properly.
Hydrocolloid patches are exempt from the one-medication constraint

A plain hydrocolloid patch carries no active — it works by absorbing exudate and maintaining a moist environment. The OTC acne monograph constraint at REV-0325 forbids stacking topical acne MEDICATIONS; a dressing is not one.

This is the only product class in Master 10 that can be layered with an acne medication. A genuinely useful exception that would be lost if patches were modelled as ordinary formulated products. Caveat: microdart and salicylic variants DO carry actives and lose the exemption — verify the specific variant.
The only product verified with no gating exclusions at all
Tower 28 SOS: three ingredients, no acids, no retinoids, no fragrance, no preservative, no botanical, no niacinamide. Nothing in the database's exclusion set applies to it.

Worth marking explicitly. For a member mid-reaction or immediately post-procedure, a product that trips zero gates is the practical answer, and the engine should be able to find it by that property rather than by category.
Benzoyl peroxide bleaches hair and dyed fabrics — printed warning
Differin's full Drug Facts panel states: avoid contact with hair and dyed fabrics, which may be bleached by this product. Regulatory labelling, not brand copy.

Propagated to all 3 benzoyl peroxide products in the database. A practical, member-facing fact no other product class carries — towels, pillowcases and hair. Belongs in usage guidance for the whole BPO class, and it is the kind of detail that determines whether someone keeps using a product.
The label itself says lower concentration reduces irritation
Differin's panel states: irritation may be reduced by using the product less frequently OR IN A LOWER CONCENTRATION.

This moves REV-0335 from inference to label-supported: the monograph treats lower strength as a legitimate route to tolerability, so 10% BPO must not be ranked above 4% by default. Strengthens the general rule that concentration is not a quality ordering.
Three products, same active, same dose, three philosophies

All three deliver 10% sulfur: De La Cruz in 2 ingredients, Kate Somerville EradiKate in 8 led by isopropyl alcohol with camphor, Sunday Riley Saturn in 34 with essential oils and ten botanicals. The premium-priced options are the harsher ones.

A clean natural experiment for the simplicity attribute proposed at REV-0337. Same active and dose holds efficacy roughly constant, so the differences are entirely formulation. For a reactive perimenopausal member the ranking is the inverse of price.
EradiKate exists as a 10% sulfur Blemish Treatment and a 3% sulfur Daily Foaming Cleanser — threefold strength difference, entirely different formulas. The source name specified neither.
Scoped to the 10% treatment. Unversioned names remain the most common naming defect in this database.
The Ordinary has produced a naming or version problem in four masters

Buffet became Multi-Peptide (Master 08). Glycolic Acid 7% exists as Toning Solution and Exfoliating Toner (09). Salicylic Acid 2% exists as Solution and Anhydrous Solution, plus a reformulation (09). Hyaluronic Acid 2% + B5 now exists at 17 and 23 ingredients, the latter retailing as "with Ceramides" (14).

The standing rule at REV-0299 — resolve this brand by INCI, never by name — is confirmed as necessary. Apply it as a brand-level flag now that the brand column is populated (REV-0315), so the rule fires automatically rather than being remembered.
A row containing only a brand name
SKP-0305 in Master 19C has product_name "Vanicream" — a manufacturer, not a product. Four Vanicream products are already verified elsewhere in the database.

Distinct from the generic-category defect: those name a product TYPE, this names only a brand. Resolution is to attach the Master 19C membership to an existing Vanicream record via Product_Master_Links, not to carry a fifth row. Add to import checks: flag any product_name that matches a known brand token and nothing else.
Five molecular weights of HA is one active, not five
The Ordinary HA 2% + B5 carries sodium hyaluronate, hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid and sodium hyaluronate crosspolymer — a molecular-weight delivery strategy, not multiple humectants.

Same trap as the five fruit extracts in Naturium's glycolic gel (REV-0320) and the seven token actives in Topicals Faded (REV-0248). An ingredient-counting engine over-reads all three. The general rule: count MECHANISMS, not ingredient names.
Most eye products in this database are not ophthalmologically tested

Three periorbital products now assessed: Colorescience Total Eye is explicitly ophthalmologist reviewed and cleared for eyelids and contact lens wearers; Supergoop Bright-Eyed carries the standard keep-out-of-eyes warning; The Ordinary Caffeine Solution directs twice-daily application around the eyes with no testing claim at all.

One of three sits on the substantiated side. The imbalance is the finding — the gating rule at REV-0166 will exclude most of the eye master, which is the correct outcome but needs Emma to know before it surprises her. Verify the remaining five 19A products against the same criterion before any periorbital logic is written.
A genuine AHA correctly not counted as an exfoliant
Lactic acid sits fifteenth in the Caffeine Solution — a free AHA by identity, a pH adjuster by position. The rule at REV-0305 correctly does not fire the photosensitivity tail.

More useful as validation than the citric acid cases, because lactic acid IS an exfoliating AHA elsewhere in this database at high position. Same molecule, opposite classification, decided purely on position. Urea at nine behaves the same way — humectant here, keratolytic at high concentration.
The brand's own site contradicts its printed INCI
theordinary.com names Epigallocatechin Gallatyl Glucoside as a key ingredient; the printed INCI lists Epigallocatechin Gallate. Different molecules — the glucoside is a stabilised derivative.
Sixth instance of marketing copy diverging from the ingredient list, and the first from the MANUFACTURER rather than a retailer. Reinforces REV-0273: parse INCI blocks only, including on brand sites.
Second regional-variant finding — silicone status flips by market

Toleriane Dermallergo Eye ships as two formulas. The EU version is silicone-free with cellulose, corn starch, Salvia miltiorrhiza and Sphingomonas ferment; the AU/APAC version drops all four and adds dimethicone, polymethylsilsesquioxane, dimethiconol and aluminum starch octenylsuccinate.

A member avoiding silicones gets opposite answers depending on where she bought it. Second regional variant after SkinCeuticals Discoloration Defense (REV-0242), same shape. Worth a market field on the record rather than treating regional lists as alternatives to reconcile — they are both correct, for different bottles.
Growth-factor products in the eye master carry TWO unresolved rulings

Neocutis Lumière FIRM and CALECIM Eye Contour are conditioned-media growth-factor products applied periorbitally. The growth-factor ruling (REV-0260) and the periorbital substantiation rule (REV-0166) both apply.

Periorbital skin is the thinnest on the face with the highest absorption, and these are marketed for post-periocular-procedure use. Blocked pending both rulings. Worth noting that where two open rulings intersect, the product should be blocked rather than assessed under whichever resolves first.
Periorbital substantiation now two of four

Substantiated: Colorescience Total Eye, La Roche-Posay Toleriane Dermallergo Eye (both ophthalmologically tested, both explicitly cleared for eyelids). Unsubstantiated: Supergoop Bright-Eyed, The Ordinary Caffeine Solution.

Better than the one-of-three position at REV-0349, and it establishes that ophthalmologically tested eye products do exist in the database. The rule will still exclude a majority of Master 19A but not all of it, which makes it usable rather than merely restrictive.
Multi-formula cells were corrupting position-based derivation

Three rows held two or three regional or legacy formulas concatenated into one ingredient_list cell — SkinCeuticals C E Ferulic (3), Discoloration Defense (2), Toleriane Dermallergo Eye (2). Every position-based rule in this database reads that cell, so ingredient positions were computed across the join and were wrong for all three.

Split into ingredient_list (one formula) plus variant_formulas and primary_market, then re-derived. Fourth instance of my own annotation or formatting choices defeating a derivation, after product_name annotations, ingredient_list prefixes and entity-type exclusions. The standing lesson holds: any field a derivation reads must contain exactly one thing.
The periorbital rule needs three states, not two

SkinCeuticals A.G.E. Advanced Eye directs application under the eye along the orbital bone and around the brow, and states DO NOT APPLY DIRECTLY TO EYELIDS. That is neither 'cleared for eyelids' nor 'no substantiation stated'.

Replace the binary rule at REV-0166 with three states: (a) substantiated for eyelids, (b) eye area but explicitly not eyelids, (c) no substantiation stated. State (b) is the most immediately useful — brand-stated, precise, applicable without any pending ruling, and it tells a member exactly where the product goes rather than simply excluding it.
Anhydrous is necessary but not sufficient for post-procedure use
A.G.E. Advanced Eye is water-free (hexyl laurate first) yet still carries phenoxyethanol and chlorphenesin, plus alcohol and a cooling agent.

Confirms the two-condition form of the rule at REV-0339: no preservative system AND (anhydrous OR isotonic at physiological pH). Anhydrous alone would have wrongly admitted this product. Useful negative case — the rule now has two positive examples and one counter-example.
Optical diffusion is not a biological effect

The formula contains titanium dioxide, synthetic fluorphlogopite and boron nitride as optical diffusers. The brand's immediate 12% dark-circle improvement is presumably optical blur rather than a change in the skin.

Separate optical from biological effect in efficacy grading. A member should know that part of the result washes off — relevant to how outcomes are logged in the Outcome Engine, since an optical effect will not persist between applications and would otherwise read as regression.
A merge marked RESOLVED had never actually been executed

REV-0214 identified SkinMedica TNS Advanced+ as a duplicate of SKP-0138 and was written up as RESOLVED. The merge was never performed. The fuzzy sweep at REV-0324 then skipped it precisely because it was already marked resolved.

Now executed. The lesson generalises: a finding recorded as RESOLVED without the action being taken is worse than one left OPEN, because nothing re-checks it. Audit the queue for other items marked RESOLVED whose effect is not visible in the data — this is the only class of error the sweeps cannot catch by construction.

"Endonuclease-containing SPF" and "Conventional high-quality SPF" (Master 15), "Broad-spectrum facial/body SPFs" (19C) and "Skinbetter AlphaRet" (11) were typed Finished Product. The first three name technology or quality classes; the fourth names a product family whose three members are all already verified and materially different.

All four resolve against records already in the database rather than needing new verification — ISDIN for the endonuclease row, Master 04 for the SPF rows, and SKP-0109/0110/0111 for AlphaRet. Note the broad-spectrum SPF category appears as three separate rows across Masters 19C, 19E and 19F; resolve those together.
Review items are now mechanically auditable

The RESOLVED audit prompted by REV-0359 could only check items that named product IDs; items describing their effect in prose were unverifiable. That is exactly how an unexecuted merge stayed hidden for eight versions. An affected_ids column has been added and backfilled on 333 items.

All 29 RESOLVED items now check out against the data. Going forward, no item should be marked RESOLVED without affected_ids populated — it makes the queue a verifiable record rather than a narrative one, which matters because the queue is the handover artefact for anyone else working on this database.
Audit must treat DELETED rows as a valid resolution

Three RESOLVED items (REV-0269, REV-0314, REV-0323) reference product IDs that no longer exist in Products_Canonical. They were the evidence-table fragments deliberately deleted and preserved in Evidence_Fragments. A naive audit reads a missing ID as an unexecuted action.

The audit now distinguishes three outcomes: id present and changed (executed), id absent because the row was deliberately deleted (executed, annotated), and id absent with no deletion record (genuine failure). Only the third is a problem. Without that distinction the audit would have generated three false alarms every run and been ignored.
(queue-wide rule change; affects review items REV-0269, REV-0314, REV-0323 — no product rows)
Vaseline is the floor case for formulation simplicity
One ingredient. The database now spans the full range: Vaseline at 1, De La Cruz Sulfur at 2, Tower 28 SOS at 3, up to Kate Somerville ExfoliKate at 38.

Makes the simplicity attribute (REV-0337) concrete rather than relative. For a member in an acute reactive state, a single-ingredient occlusive is the recommendation that cannot fail on tolerability — and it is the cheapest product held. Surface it as the fallback when every other option is gated out, so gating exhaustion produces an answer rather than silence.
Legacy ceramide numbering and a real variance in one product

CeraVe Therapeutic Hand Cream appears with Ceramide 3 / 6-II / 1 in one source and Ceramide NP / AP / EOP in another — the same three molecules under two naming conventions, not a reformulation. The same alternate list ALSO adds cyclomethicone and hexyl laurate, which is a genuine difference.

Both effects in one product. Exactly why the INCI synonym table at REV-0234 must exist before any reformulation flag is trusted: without it this reads as one change when it is really a naming artefact plus a separate real one.
Ladder endpoints created and ladder_id added

The three known missing rungs are now records: Medik8 Crystal Retinal 1 (SKP-0341, logged at REV-0224 and unactioned since), Geek & Gorgeous A-Game 5 (SKP-0342), and The Ordinary Salicylic Acid 2% Anhydrous Solution (SKP-0343). A ladder_id field groups 13 ladders explicitly.

The name-similarity detector could only find ladders with two rungs already present — it was structurally incapable of spotting a ladder missing an endpoint, which is the case REV-0309 identified as systematic. ladder_id makes completeness checkable directly. It also protects ladders from the fuzzy duplicate sweep, which flags siblings as near-matches and must never merge them.
A stub was excluded from its own ladder by my naming

SKP-0336 was created as "SkinCeuticals Retinol 0.3 Refining Night Cream" while its siblings are "SkinCeuticals Retinol 0.5" and "1.0". The extra words changed the name stem, so the ladder detector grouped only two of the three rungs.

Normalised. Fifth instance of my own naming or formatting choices defeating a derivation, after product_name annotations, ingredient_list prefixes, entity-type exclusions and multi-formula cells. ladder_id removes the dependence on naming entirely, which is the durable fix rather than another correction.
The anhydrous salicylic record resolves a blocking ambiguity

SKP-0174 could not be verified because "The Ordinary Salicylic Acid 2% Solution" denotes two products sold side by side — water-based and anhydrous — with different penetration, tolerability and layering behaviour.

Creating the second record resolves REV-0300 rather than leaving one row to mean two products. The anhydrous version is also a candidate for the post-procedure eligibility test at REV-0339, since anhydrous is one branch of that rule.
Ladder selection must precede rung selection

Crystal Retinal 1 is the gentlest rung by strength and still carries tonka bean, vanilla and coumarin — the same fragrance materials as every other rung, because they are a property of the base, not the active. Fragrance load does not fall as you descend a strength ladder.

An engine that models "start gentle" as "lowest rung" will send a fragrance-sensitive member confidently to the wrong product. Select the LADDER on tolerability first (Geek & Gorgeous, same retinal architecture, no coumarin), then the RUNG on strength. Within-ladder gentleness and cross-ladder tolerability are different axes.
The post-procedure rule now has all four cases

Anhydrous + preservative-free (Alastin Nectar) passes. Aqueous + isotonic + preservative-free (Tower 28 SOS) passes. Anhydrous + preserved (SkinCeuticals A.G.E. Advanced Eye, and now The Ordinary Salicylic Anhydrous) fails.

Every combination is now covered by a worked example, so the rule at REV-0339 is ready to build rather than still being generalised from cases. Derive as: no preservative system AND (anhydrous OR isotonic at physiological pH).
Vehicle sets ladder position at identical concentration

The Ordinary positions the ANHYDROUS 2% salicylic as suited to new BHA users. An oil-phase vehicle slows delivery relative to an aqueous one at the same 2%, so the gentler product is the anhydrous one.

Two products at identical stated concentration sit at different points on a beginner-to-advanced ladder purely on vehicle. Delivery system (REV-0316) is a tolerability lever, not only a potency one — and the ladder_id grouping should span vehicle variants, not just strengths.
One growth-factor product is both post-procedure eligible and regulatorily unblocked

BIOEFFECT EGF Serum has seven ingredients, no preservative system, and a saline-plus-buffer construction — so it passes the post-procedure test by the isotonic route. And because its EGF is a plant-expressed recombinant peptide rather than conditioned media (REV-0272), it is not caught by the growth-factor ruling at REV-0260.

The only product in the database with that combination, and directly relevant to the procedure prep and recovery wedge. It would have been lost entirely if "growth factor" had been modelled as one category — which is the concrete payoff of the three-way split at REV-0272.
A ladder where one rung is post-procedure eligible and another is not
